subject: Impact of Temporary Emigration/Availability on Occupancy

messages.author: 17ec17bb9a17e7a2
messages.subject: Impact of Temporary Emigration/Availability on Occupancy
parts:
Does the R package 'unmarked' include a model for correcting parameter estimates (e.g. occupancy, density or abundance) with estimates of availability/temporary emigration?

I have a species with...
- binomial detection history (0s and 1s)
- estimate of detection probability based on detection/non-detection surveys
- estimate of availability rate based on experimental detection trials

I would like to compare parameter estimates (ideally occupancy) with and without accounting for the estimate of availability. 

This sounds simple, but I have not been able to interpret the code for the various models which seem suitable. Would occuMS, gmultmix or gpcount work?

messages.author: 02d195331194f5bd
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Impact of Temporary Emigration/Availability on Occupancy
parts:
Someone correct me I'm wrong, but I don't think occupancy models that account for availability are incorporated into the main software packages. Folks have written their own models (e.g. 1, 2), so you could go that (more difficult) route. It would also be helpful to know more about how you collected your data. What was the sampling design? How did you estimate detection probability and availability rate?

For what it's worth, gdistsamp, gmultmix, and gpcount are all versions of N-mixture models (for abundance, not presence) that are intended to address some forms of availability. occuMS allows for different classes of animals (e.g. breeding vs. non-breeding), but you'd still need to be able to detect organisms in each of the classes in order to use the model.  

Philip Shirk

messages.author: 17ec17bb9a17e7a2
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Impact of Temporary Emigration/Availability on Occupancy
parts:
Hi Philip,

Presence-absence data for the focal species and the occu function from Unmarked we’re used to estimate detection probability. Availability rate was estimated using experimental detection trials, where we replicated the presence-absence surveys with telemetered animals and were able to classify how often they were available for detection (above or below ground).

Yes, I looked into OccuMS and came to the same conclusion. The matrix of detection states won’t work if the other “state” is availability (I.e impossible to detect). I’ll check out the sources you cited and get back to you! Thanks for your help!

messages.author: 7ac258fb6a0ab492
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Impact of Temporary Emigration/Availability on Occupancy
parts:
Hi there,
I'm not 100% clear on how the data were collected in this particular case, but the general "multi-scale" occupancy model (also known as the multi-method model) that allows separation of availability and detection probability is available in MARK/RMark and Presence/RPresence. I'm speaking of the likelihood formulation described in described in Nichols et al. 2008 (attached). There is also an R package called "eDNAoccupancy" (Dorazio & Erickson 2017, also attached) that fits this model in a Bayesian framework. I haven't used that package so I'm not certain how flexible it is, but it might be adaptable to what you are looking for.

Best,
Brittany

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Impact of Temporary Emigration/Availability on Occupancy
parts:
Hi all,

there is also the neat paper by Mordecai et al (2011; see https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-2664.2010.01921.x) that describes a two-level model that distinguishes availability from perception, given availability. They fit the model in BUGS. In Chapter 10 of the AHM1 book we also discuss this model and give code for it (which, btw, you can download from the book website for free)

Best regards  -- Marc
